title: Sine & cosine rules
examples: When should I use the sine rule instead of the cosine rule?
How do I know if there are two possible answers for an angle?
What is the difference between the sine rule and the cosine rule?

explain.say: Today we learn two rules for triangles. These rules help when the triangle is not a right triangle. We use the sine rule and the cosine rule for this.

You use the sine rule when you know a side and the sine of its opposite angle. This is often called the side-angle-sine case. For example, if you know side a, and angle A, and side a divided by the sine of A, that is the sine rule.

items: Use Sine Rule: a/sin A = b/sin B

draw.text: Sine Rule: a/sin A = b/sin B

explain.say: You use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the angle between them. This is called the side-angle-side case. For example, if you know sides a and b, and the angle C between them, you find side c using the cosine rule.

items: Use Cosine Rule: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C

draw.text: Cosine Rule: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C

explain.say: The ambiguous case happens when you use the sine rule and only know two sides and a non-included angle. You must check for two possible triangles. You check if the sine of the angle is greater than the sine of the angle you found.

faq.q: When do I use the sine rule versus the cosine rule?
faq.a: Use the sine rule when you have a side and the sine of its opposite angle. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
asks: Which rule is better for finding an angle?
Do I always use the sine rule first?

faq.q: What is the ambiguous case in trigonometry?
faq.a: It is a situation using the sine rule where you might find two possible triangles that fit the given information. You must check if both possibilities are valid.
asks: How do I know if there are two answers?
Is the ambiguous case only with the sine rule?

faq.q: If I have three sides, which rule do I use?
faq.a: If you have three sides, you should use the cosine rule to find any angle. You can use the rearranged cosine rule for this.
asks: Can I use the sine rule with three sides?
What if I only know the sides?

faq.q: Does the sine rule only work for acute angles?
faq.a: No, the sine rule works for all angles in a triangle, including obtuse angles. The sine function handles these correctly.
asks: Does sine change for big angles?
Is there a limit on the angles?

faq.a: SSA stands for side-side-angle. This is the arrangement that causes the ambiguous case when using the sine rule.
asks: What does SSA mean in trigonometry?

facts: The sine rule relates the ratio of a side's length to the sine of its opposite angle.
The cosine rule is useful when you know two sides and the included angle.
The ambiguous case occurs when using the sine rule with SSA information.
The cosine rule formula for side c is c squared equals a squared plus b squared minus two ab cosine C.

quiz.say: Given sides 5 and 8, and the angle between them is 60 degrees, what is the third side?
quiz.why: This setup has two sides and the included angle, so the cosine rule must be used.

wrong.0: This is the answer if you incorrectly use the Pythagorean theorem, forgetting the angle.
wrong.1: This is the answer if you incorrectly use the sine rule instead of the cosine rule.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake if you forget to subtract the final term in the cosine rule.

quiz.say: If you know side a, side b, and angle A, what rule should you check first?
quiz.why: Knowing a side and its opposite angle suggests using the sine rule first.

wrong.0: This theorem only works for right-angled triangles.
wrong.1: This is another name for the cosine rule, but the sine rule is more direct here.
wrong.3: The cosine rule needs the angle to be between the two known sides.

quiz.say: If you are given sides 10 and 12, and the angle opposite the side of length 10 is 30 degrees, what must you check for?

options.show: It must be a right triangle
options.say: It must be a right triangle

options.show: The cosine rule must be used
options.say: The cosine rule must be used

quiz.why: This is the SSA case, which means you must check if two different triangles are possible.

wrong.1: The SSA case often leads to more than one possible solution.
wrong.2: The sine and cosine rules apply to general triangles, not just right ones.
wrong.3: The cosine rule requires the angle to be between the two known sides.
